question:
(a) Prove that $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\tan^{-1}x$ for $x>-1$, explaining the importance of the stated restriction.

(b) Hence evaluate $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-\sqrt{3}}{1+\sqrt{3}}\right)$.
explanation:
(a)
Let
$$A=\tan^{-1}x$$
Then $A\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Using the tangent-difference formula,
$$\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-A\right)=\frac{1-\tan A}{1+\tan A}$$
Therefore,
$$\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-A\right)=\frac{1-x}{1+x}$$
When $x>-1$, we have $A> -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Hence,
$$-\frac{\pi}{4}<\frac{\pi}{4}-A<\frac{\pi}{2}$$
Thus, $\dfrac{\pi}{4}-A$ lies in the principal-value range of $\tan^{-1}$. Applying $\tan^{-1}$ gives
$$\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)=\frac{\pi}{4}-A$$
Therefore,
$$\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)=\frac{\pi}{4}-\tan^{-1}x$$
The restriction $x>-1$ ensures both that $1+x\neq0$ and that the angle on the right belongs to the principal range of $\tan^{-1}$.

(b)
Taking $x=\sqrt{3}$ in the identity,
$$\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3}}{1+\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{\pi}{4}-\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3})$$
Since
$$\tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3})=\frac{\pi}{3}$$
we obtain
$$\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3}}{1+\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{3}=-\frac{\pi}{12}$$
Hence, the required value is $-\dfrac{\pi}{12}$.

options.A:
(a) For $x>-1$, the identity is $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\tan^{-1}x$, and the restriction keeps the right side in the principal range

(b) $-\dfrac{\pi}{12}$
